title: Humanity's first look at the surface of Mars shared on 50th anniversary of historic NASA landing — Space photo of the week
summary: NASA has released the historic images taken by Viking 1 just after its July 20, 1976 landing on Mars, shared on the 50th anniversary. The first surface photo, transmitted about 40 minutes after touchdown, revealed a rocky, dusty terrain. Viking's mission — two landers and two orbiters — transformed Mars exploration and left an unresolved debate over potential biological signals in its life-detection experiments, a question still revisited by later discoveries.
content:
NASA has unearthed the historic photos its Viking 1 lander sent home just after landing on Mars in July 1976.

About 40 minutes after it landed on Mars on July 20, 1976, NASA's Viking 1 lander sent this first photo from the surface of the Red Planet. The image was shared on July 20, 2026, marking the 50th anniversary of the landing.

Viking 1 had been programmed to take its first image just 25 seconds after touchdown. It occurred at 7:53 a.m. EDT on July 20, 1976 — exactly seven years after Apollo 11 landed on the Moon. The landing had been delayed from earlier plans, including a hoped-for coincidence with the U.S. Bicentennial, while mission teams searched for a suitably flat landing zone.

Although the spacecraft landed safely at Chryse Planitia, north of the equator, mission controllers still had to wait another 19 minutes for the radio signal confirming success to cross the 212 million miles between Mars and Earth.

Forty minutes after touchdown, the confirming image began appearing on monitors at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory, slowly building line by line from left to right. Dr. Thomas Mutch, leader of the Viking lander imaging team, remembered the moment vividly: "I studied the black screen, waiting for that narrow strip that will signal the first few lines of the first picture," he said. "Rocks and sand are visible and — finally at the far right — one of the spacecraft foot pads, a symbolic artifact that stamps our accomplishment with the sign of reality … Time and time again I repeat, 'It's incredible.'"

The image revealed a solid, slightly rocky surface, with dust and pebbles thrown up by the landing already settling back onto the spacecraft. Viking's first color image came the next day, with a panorama following a few days later.

The Viking mission actually consisted of four spacecraft: two orbiters and two landers. Viking 1 was joined six weeks later on the surface by Viking 2, which landed in Utopia Planitia, also in the northern hemisphere. Meanwhile, the two orbiters mapped Mars and relayed data — including more than 52,000 orbital images and 4,500 photographs from the surface — back to Earth.

Viking transformed our understanding of Mars, but its most intriguing scientific result remains unresolved. The landers carried the first experiments designed to detect life directly in Martian soil. Although the mission's official conclusion was that no convincing evidence of life had been found, some scientists have continued to argue that one of the experiments produced a genuine biological signal; others argue that Viking's experiments destroyed the very evidence of life that they sought to detect. Discoveries by later missions — including organic molecules detected by Curiosity and perchlorate salts found by Phoenix — have prompted some researchers to revisit the Viking data.

Viking 1 fell silent in 1982, two years after Viking 2, following a software error during an update. The intrepid spacecraft showed humanity the surface of another planet for the first time, but whether Viking 1 also found the first hints of life off-Earth remains one of planetary science's most enduring mysteries.

Jamie Carter is a Cardiff, U.K.-based freelance science journalist and a regular contributor to Live Science. His work appears in Space.com, Forbes, New Scientist, BBC Sky at Night, Sky & Telescope and other science and astronomy publications.
